01.note: A man was selling silk strips worth five ma'a. He asked six, though he would have taken five and a half. A buyer reasoned that if he bargained down to five and a half, he would count as having waived any claim, so he paid the full six, planning to sue for the overcharge. The case came before Rava, who ruled that the rule against overcharging covers only buying from a merchant; one who buys from an ordinary homeowner has no such claim.
01.why: This is the first of two matching cases that limit the overcharging rule to merchants. The Gemara next tells an identical case decided by Rav Hisda, then tests both rulings against the mishna, which says the rule applies to laymen as well.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came, and who ruled against the buyer.

terms.meaning: A small silver coin used in the prices here.
Selling something for more, or buying it for less, than its market value. Torah law forbids it, and the wronged party may reclaim the difference.

02.note: A man was selling jewelry worth fifty ma'a. He asked sixty, though he would have taken fifty-five. A buyer reasoned that if he paid fifty-five he would count as having waived any claim, so he paid the full sixty, planning to sue for the overcharge. The case came before Rav Hisda, who ruled that the rule against overcharging covers only buying from a merchant; one who buys from an ordinary homeowner has no such claim.
02.why: It repeats Rava's ruling in the silk case just before it. Rav Dimi and Rabbi Elazar then call the ruling correct, and the Gemara challenges it from a mishna that applies the overcharging rule to laymen; Rav Hisda answers that the mishna means goods made for sale.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came, and who ruled against the buyer.

terms.meaning: A small silver coin used in the prices here.
Selling something for more, or buying it for less, than its market value. Torah law forbids it, and the wronged party may reclaim the difference.

03.note: Arguing that a certain oven could not become ritually impure, Rabbi Eliezer called on miracles: a carob tree uprooted itself, a stream flowed backward, the study hall's walls began to fall, and a Divine Voice sided with him. Rabbi Yehoshua replied, 'It is not in heaven,' and Elijah later told Rabbi Natan that God smiled and said, 'My children have triumphed over Me.' The Sages burned what Rabbi Eliezer had ruled pure and ostracized him; Rabbi Akiva, dressed in black, broke the news gently. Rabbi Eliezer wept, crops were struck, and Rabban Gamliel nearly drowned at sea. His sister Imma Shalom, Rabbi Eliezer's wife, kept her husband from prayers of supplication, but one day found him praying and said he had killed her brother; just then a shofar announced Rabban Gamliel's death.
03.why: The Gemara brings this story while discussing verbal mistreatment. Imma Shalom's last words, that the gates of Heaven stay open to the prayers of the mistreated, tie it to that theme, and the discussion then turns to mistreating converts.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Also called Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus; he ruled the oven pure, was outvoted and ostracized.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Scolded the leaning walls and answered the Divine Voice: 'It is not in heaven.'

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's beloved disciple, who went to tell him of his ostracism.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the Sages who ostracized Rabbi Eliezer; brother of Imma Shalom.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife and Rabban Gamliel's sister.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; here, which side's ruling is binding.
A voice from Heaven that announces a message to people on earth.
Formally shunned by the community; others had to keep four cubits (about two meters) away from him.
The tahanun prayer of supplication and pleading, said with the head lowered.

03.flag: The story's opening, Rabbi Eliezer offering every argument and the Rabbis rejecting them, sits in the BEFORE segment, so the STORY span starts mid-scene.

04.note: Wine was brought to Rava from a store. He diluted it with water, tasted it, found it not tasty, and sent it back to the store. Abaye challenged him: the mishna says one may not sell such wine to a merchant even if he is told. Rava answered that his dilution was obvious to anyone, and that if one worried the storekeeper might add wine to sweeten it and resell it, there would be no end to the matter.
04.why: The mishna forbids selling wine mixed with water to a merchant even with a warning, since he may pass it on deceptively. This incident tests that rule against Rava's own practice and narrows it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sent diluted wine back to the store it came from.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Challenged Rava by quoting the mishna.

terms.meaning: The early code of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments; here, the passage on selling wine mixed with water.
Wine was normally drunk mixed with water; Rava mixed in water before drinking it.

05.note: An elderly slave dyed his hair and beard to look younger and asked Rava to buy him. Rava declined, citing the saying 'Let the poor be members of your household.' The slave then went to Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, who bought him. One day Rav Pappa asked him for water; the slave whitened his hair and beard and said, 'See, I am older than your father.' Rav Pappa applied to himself the verse 'The righteous is delivered from trouble, and another comes in his stead.'
05.why: The mishna forbids adorning a person, an animal or goods to make them look better before a sale. The Gemara asks what adorning a person means, and this slave's dyed hair is its example.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Declined to buy the slave.

people.name: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel
people.about: Bought the slave and found out he was older than he looked.

06.note: Rabbi Yehuda told the Sages of an incident: Baitos ben Zunin made a sale of his field on the instruction of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and the buyer ate the field's produce. The Sages answered that this proved nothing, since in that case it was the seller, not the buyer, who ate the produce.
06.why: A baraita rules that when a debtor sells his field to his creditor until the debt is paid, the creditor may not eat its produce, as that is like interest; Rabbi Yehuda permits it and cites this case as proof, which the Sages read the other way.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who permits the buyer to eat the produce, and tells this incident as proof.

people.name: Baitos ben Zunin
people.about: Made a sale of his field.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Gave the instruction for the sale.

terms.meaning: The crops the field yields while the arrangement lasts.
A teaching of the early Sages that was left out of the mishna, the core code of Jewish law.

07.note: Rav Yosef bar Hama used to seize the slaves of people who owed him money and make them work for him. His son Rava asked him why he did this. He answered that he followed Rav Nahman, who said a slave is not worth even the bread in his stomach. The story breaks off here, before Rava's reply.
07.why: Rav Nahman has just ruled that a lender who lives in his borrower's courtyard must pay rent, so it will not look like interest. This case applies the same worry to a lender who puts his debtors' slaves to work.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: Rava's father, who seized his debtors' slaves and made them work.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Yosef bar Hama's son, who questioned the practice.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage whose saying the father relied on.

07.flag: The STORY ends mid-exchange; Rava's rebuttal and his father's retraction ('I retract') are in the AFTER segments.

08.note: Rav Nahman decided a case in the Exilarch's court according to his own view, and Rav Yehuda tore up the resulting deed. The Exilarch told Rav Nahman, 'Rav Yehuda tore up your document.' Rav Nahman replied, 'Did a child tear it up? A great man tore it up; he must have seen a reason.' In another version he said, 'A child tore it up, for everyone is a child compared to me in monetary law.'
08.why: Rav Huna and Rav Nahman disagree over whether a lender who adds a forfeit-the-field condition after making the loan acquires the whole field. This is Rav Nahman acting on his view; right after it he retracts, persuaded that such a condition does not bind.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Decided the case in the Exilarch's court.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Tore up the deed Rav Nahman's ruling produced.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: In whose court Rav Nahman ruled; he reported the tearing to Rav Nahman.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who kept his own court.
The written document giving the lender ownership of the field.

09.note: A man sold land with a guarantee: if his creditors seized it from the buyer, he would repay the buyer. The buyer asked to be repaid from the seller's very best land; the seller refused, wanting to keep that, but agreed to repay from his other good land. In the end creditors did seize the field, and meanwhile a flood swept away the seller's best land. The story does not say how the case was decided.
09.why: The Gemara has been discussing promises that do not bind. Here it asks whether the seller's promise of his 'other good land' still holds now that the flood has made it his best; Rav Pappa says yes and Rav Aha of Difti objects.

terms.meaning: The seller's promise to pay the buyer back if the seller's own creditors take the land to cover his debts.

09.flag: The STORY stops before the dispute: the seller's refusal to pay from his remaining good land, and Rav Pappa's view, are in the AFTER segment.

10.note: A woman asked a man to buy land for her from her relatives, and he did. The relative who sold it asked the agent, 'If I have money later, will you give it back to me?' The agent answered, 'You and she are relatives.' Rabba bar Rav Huna said that whenever the reply is 'you and she are relatives,' the seller is relying on working it out within the family, so he never fully resolved to transfer the land.
10.why: Because the sale was never final and the land goes back, the Gemara uses this case to ask whether the produce the buyer ate meanwhile counts as interest; Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rava rule it is only a 'hint of interest' that a court cannot take back.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who ruled on what the agent's answer meant.

terms.meaning: Someone acting on another's behalf; here the man who bought the land for the woman.

11.note: Rav Elazar of Hagronya bought an animal and gave it to his sharecropper to fatten, paying him the head as wages plus half the profit. The sharecropper's wife told him that as a partner in the purchase he would get the tail too. So next time he bought an animal jointly with Rabbi Elazar, who gave him half the tail but then proposed splitting the head as well. When the sharecropper protested, Rabbi Elazar explained: before, the money was all his own, and without a little extra pay it would have looked like interest; now they were partners, and a sharecropper customarily works a little extra for the owner.
11.why: Rav and Shmuel have been debating how a man fattening another's calf must be paid so the deal is not interest, including Rav's idea of giving him the head. This case shows the extra payment is needed only when one side puts up all the money.

people.name: Rav Elazar of Hagronya
people.about: Bought an animal and gave it to his sharecropper to fatten; also called Rabbi Elazar.

terms.meaning: A worker who farms or tends someone else's property in return for a share of what it produces.
Payment for the use of money. Torah law forbids it between Jews, so any extra benefit to the one who supplied the money is suspect.

12.note: Two Samaritans ran a joint business. One divided their money without the other's knowledge, and Rav Pappa saw no loss, citing Rav Nahman: money counts as already divided. The next year they bought wine together, and the other partner divided it on his own; this time Rav Pappa asked him, 'Who divided it for you?' The man complained that Rav Pappa was pursuing him. Rav Pappa explained: when the money was split, nobody took the good coins and left the poor ones, but everyone knows some wine is sweet and some is not.
12.why: Abaye has just challenged a man who split animal offspring on his own, asking 'Who divided it for you?' These cases show when a partner may divide shared property alone; the Gemara then limits Rav Nahman's rule to coins of the same kind.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge who heard both cases.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage Rav Pappa quoted: money counts as already divided.

terms.meaning: A community living in the Land of Israel that kept its own form of Israelite religion, apart from the Jews.

13.note: Rav Hama used to rent out dinars, charging a peshita a day for each one, reasoning that this was no different from renting out a hoe. All his money was lost. The Gemara explains his error: a hoe comes back itself and its wear is known, but coins do not come back as the same coins, and their wear cannot be known.
13.why: The Gemara is sorting out what counts as forbidden interest. This case draws the line between renting an object, which is allowed, and 'renting' money, which is really a loan with interest; Rava next allows paying a third party to arrange a loan.

people.name: Rav Hama
people.about: Rented out coins for a daily fee, and lost all his money.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.
A small coin; the translation gives it as one-eighth of a dinar.

14.note: Rav Anan told Rav Nahman of a kettle that belonged to the children of Mar Ukva and was kept at Mar Shmuel's house. Mar Shmuel would weigh it before renting it out and weigh it again when it came back, and he charged both a rental fee and the value of the metal it had lost, although normally one charges one or the other, not both.
14.why: Rav Anan had quoted Shmuel as allowing interest on orphans' money, and Rav Nahman demanded the actual case. Rav Nahman answers that charging rent plus lost weight is allowed even for adults, since the owners bear the copper's wear.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Reported Shmuel's ruling and told the incident.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: Kept the kettle and rented it out on behalf of Mar Ukva's children.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Father of the children who owned the kettle; they were orphans.

terms.meaning: The loss of value as the copper kettle wore down with use, measured by weighing it.

15.note: A man mortgaged his orchard to another as security for a loan, and the lender ate its produce for three years. Then the lender threatened: sell me the orchard, or I will hide the mortgage document and say I bought it. The borrower went and transferred the orchard to his young son, and then sold it to the lender.
15.why: The Gemara rules this sale void, since the orchard was no longer the seller's, and asks whether the buyer can recover his payment from property the seller has since sold, as with a written loan. Abaye compares it to a ruling of Rabbi Asi and Rava rejects the comparison.

terms.meaning: Pledged as security for a loan; the lender held the orchard and ate its fruit until repaid.
After three years of use, a person holding land is presumed to own it, even without a deed. That is what makes the lender's threat work.

16.note: A gentile mortgaged a house to Rav Mari bar Rahel and then sold it to Rava. Rav Mari waited twelve months and then brought Rava rent, explaining that an unspecified mortgage runs a year, during which the gentile could not have removed him; from now on Rava should take rent. Rava replied that had he known the house was mortgaged to Rav Mari he would not have bought it. He would treat Rav Mari as the gentile's law would: as long as the loan was not repaid, no rent, and Rava would take none until he paid him off.
16.why: This sits in a run of cases where Sages' dealings are checked for hidden interest; Rava, just accused of taking interest himself, here refuses rent from a lender still living in the house on his loan.

people.name: Rav Mari bar Rahel
people.about: Lent money to a gentile and lived in the house the gentile mortgaged to him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Bought the mortgaged house from the gentile.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. The prohibition on interest does not bind a gentile, so a lender may live in his mortgaged house rent-free.
A mortgage with no term stated, which by default runs for one year.

17.note: Ravina used to pay the people of the fortress at Shanvata in advance for wine, and when they delivered it they poured him an extra jug. He asked Rav Ashi whether this was permitted. Rav Ashi said yes: they were simply forgoing it in his favor. Ravina objected that the land was not theirs. Rav Ashi answered that the land is pledged to the king for its tax, and the king says whoever pays the tax may eat the land's produce.
17.why: The Gemara is checking advance payments for wine for hidden interest, as in Rav Ashi's answer just before. The next case uses the same law of the kingdom for Sages who pay other people's taxes and then make them work.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Paid in advance for wine and was given an extra jug.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ruled that the extra jug was permitted.

terms.meaning: The land tax owed to the king; whoever paid it had the right to the land's produce.

18.note: The Sages told Rav Ashi that Ravina keeps every directive of the Sages. Rav Ashi sent a messenger to him just before sunset on Friday asking for a loan of ten dinars to buy a small plot of land. Ravina replied that he should bring witnesses so they could write a document. Rav Ashi asked, 'Even me?' Ravina answered, 'All the more so you, who are busy with your studies and likely to forget, and I would bring a curse upon myself.'
18.why: Rav and Reish Lakish have just taught that lending without witnesses tempts the borrower and brings a curse on the lender. Ravina's answer puts that teaching into practice, and a baraita follows listing such a lender among those whose cries go unanswered.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Asked Ravina for a loan.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Known for keeping every directive of the Sages; insisted on witnesses for the loan.

terms.meaning: Friday before sunset, the busiest time of the week as people prepare for the Sabbath.
A silver coin.

19.note: A man told others he had seen worm rot on the king's clothing. They asked him whether it was on the silver items or the gold ones. One version says he answered silver, and they killed him; another says he answered gold, and they let him be.
19.why: The mishna speaks of a rented donkey that became ill, and Rava explains the word as worm rot. This anecdote shows the same word in use.

terms.meaning: A disease caused by worms; in the Gemara's discussion, of a donkey's foot.
The translation explains these as linen and woolen garments. Worms are not found on linen, so the answer showed whether he was lying.

20.note: A man sold a donkey to another. The buyer said he would take it to a certain place: if it sold there, good; if not, he would bring it back. It did not sell, and on the way back the donkey was injured in an accident. The case came before Rav Nahman, who held the buyer liable.
20.why: A baraita just cited exempts a man returning unwanted goods if they break on the way back, as he is only like a paid guardian. Rabba objects with it, and Rav Nahman answers that this buyer would still have sold the donkey on his way back.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Judged the case and held the buyer liable.

terms.meaning: Legally required to pay for the loss.
